title: Synthcity: a benchmark framework for diverse use cases of tabular synthetic data
venue: NeurIPS 2023 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
summary: Presents synthcity, an open-source Python library that unifies benchmarking of tabular synthetic-data generators across data modalities (static, regular and irregular time series, censored survival, and composite datasets) and across use cases (fidelity, cross-domain augmentation, fairness, privacy), on the argument that the field has fragmented into specialized models with incompatible interfaces and inconsistent evaluation. The library exposes a four-step workflow of DataLoader, Plugin, generate and Metrics with a Benchmark class wrapping all four, more than 25 evaluation metrics, twelve interchangeable network architectures for time-series models, and a hyper-parameter interface compatible with Optuna. Two case studies illustrate it: eighteen OpenML datasets compare ARF, GOGGLE, TabDDPM, CTGAN and TVAE on a three-dimensional quality score and a detection score, where the tree-based ARF leads and the authors conclude tree-based generators are strong competitors to deep ones; and a COVID-19 mortality study on the Brazilian SIVEP-Gripe cohort measures minority-group AUROC after augmentation with RadialGAN, TabDDPM, CTGAN and TVAE. SDV is the closest competing library and the comparison against it carries the paper's central claim of broader coverage, running through three tables on data modalities and use cases, on supported evaluation metrics, and on supported generating algorithms. CTGAN and TVAE are additionally plugins that the paper trains and reports numbers for in both case studies, so the entry records SDV as the benchmark framework this library measures itself against and CTGAN and TVAE as generators it runs.
evidence: section 3 states that the authors compare synthcity with other popular open source libraries for synthetic data generation, naming YData Synthetic, Gretel Synthetics, SDV, DataSynthesizer, SmartNoise and nbsynthetic, and states that table 3 shows synthcity supports much broader use cases and data modalities than the alternatives because the existing libraries are solutions to a specific problem rather than benchmark frameworks; table 3 marks SDV as supporting static data, regular time series, composite data, generation and fairness (balance); table 6 lists the evaluation metrics SDV supports (total variation distance, skewness, KS test, detection linear, correct attribution probability) beside synthcity's; table 8 lists the generating algorithms, marking CTGAN as available in Synthcity, YData, SDV and nbsynthetic, TVAE in Synthcity and SDV, and Probabilistic AR in Synthcity and SDV; section 2.3 states that in the GAN family synthcity currently supports GOGGLE, CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019b), DPGAN, PATEGAN, ADSGAN and DECAF for static data, and that in the VAE family it supports TVAE (Xu et al. 2019b); section 4.1 states that synthcity allows the authors to compare ARF, GOGGLE, TabDDPM, CTGAN and TVAE over 18 OpenML datasets, with table 4 reporting CTGAN at quality 0.5475 and detection 0.7758 and TVAE at 0.5487 and 0.7389; section 4.2 compares RadialGAN, TabDDPM, CTGAN and TVAE on minority-group mortality AUROC, table 5 reporting CTGAN at 0.6477 (neural net) and 0.7507 (XgBoost) and TVAE at 0.3623 and 0.7794. NOTE on a near-duplicate: arXiv 2301.07573, 'Synthcity: facilitating innovative use cases of synthetic data in different data modalities', is a DIFFERENT record covering the same library, by Qian, Cebere and van der Schaar; Cebere is not an author here and is instead thanked in the acknowledgment for contributions made as a research engineer at the van der Schaar lab. This is a sibling work about the same software, not the preprint of this paper, so the published-version-survives rule does not apply to the pair
needs: integration call. Recorded baseline_only 4: CTGAN and TVAE are run with reported numbers in both case studies, and the SDV library is the primary comparator across three tables. The alternative is api_user 3 under the TabQueryBench precedent (open question 9), where a benchmark paper's generators are evaluation subjects rather than baselines; that reading would also require confirming whether synthcity's CTGAN and TVAE plugins wrap the sdv-dev packages or reimplement them, which the paper does not say

title: Development of Synthetic Ageing Profiling for Occupant Behaviour
venue: Proceedings of the 17th IBPSA Conference (Building Simulation 2021)
summary: A pilot study from NTU's ageing research institute that synthesizes household occupant-behaviour profiles for older adults so that building-energy simulation can proceed without collecting or distributing real survey data, which the authors describe as expensive and constrained by privacy. Survey responses from 600 Singapore participants in two cohorts (40-64 and 65 and above), recruited through senior activity centres, record demographics and daily usage times for air conditioning, fan, lighting, kettle, electric iron, washing machine, refrigerator, TV, computer and rice cooker, joined to average monthly household electricity consumption by postal code. The pipeline has three steps: generate 600 synthetic records, reduce them by three-dimensional homogeneity analysis and k-means into three personas, and simulate a year of each persona's occupancy schedule in EnergyPlus 8.9.0 against HDB building constructions. Kullback-Leibler divergence between the real and synthetic personas stays within 0.46, simulated and real annual electricity consumption differ by 0.8, 2.5 and 8.1 percent across the three personas, and the resulting energy use intensity of 48.21 kWh per square metre per year falls inside the residential range reported elsewhere, which the authors take as evidence the profiles are realistic enough for design use. CTGAN is the only generator, chosen over a plain GAN because random sampling during training under-represents minority categorical columns, and it is run from its published Python package. The entry therefore records CTGAN as the sole synthesizer of the study's data, cited to Xu et al. and linked to its PyPI distribution.
evidence: the abstract states that the study develops synthetic ageing profiling for occupant behaviour through a generative adversarial network capable of predicting electricity consumption by simulation tool (EnergyPlus), validated on 600 household profiles with two-generational cohorts, with Kullback-Leibler divergence of the synthetic and real profiling within 0.46 for a majority of parameters and clusters; the related work section states that many GAN methods of training a generator do not account for imbalance in the categorical columns and that rows falling into a minor category will not be sufficiently represented, and concludes that hence this pilot study will adopt the CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) for this synthetic transformation; the synthetic data generation section states that the objective is to develop synthetic ageing profiling for occupant behaviour by using CTAGN (the paper's own spelling of CTGAN in that sentence), and step 1 states that the authors use this CTGAN in Python to generate the synthetic data on the first step and gives the source code and user manual link https://pypi.org/project/ctgan/; step 1 also restates the CTGAN mechanism from Xu et al. 2019, that CTGAN differs from a traditional GAN in the vector fed from a standard multivariate normal distribution N(0, I); the results section states that the first step (CTGAN) has successfully generated 600 synthetic records based on the original 600 survey records; the conclusion states that the authors applied Conditional Tabular GAN to synthesize ageing profiling from integrated real survey data and that the profiling generated by CTGAN captures not only the general trend but the sociodemographic variations of actual electrical loads. NOTE: the bibliography's Goodfellow et al. (2014) GAN entry carries a DOI belonging to an unrelated JAMA Internal Medicine article, a citation defect in the paper rather than in this record

title: Workforce Forecasting with Machine Learning for Healthcare Management
summary: Forecasts physician supply and demand in Turkey to 2030 for the NACE Q sector of human health and social work activities, which the authors put at roughly 5.5 percent of national employment, on the argument that medical training is long and costly so a shortage cannot be corrected in the short term and must be planned for. OECD series covering 1979-2018 for demand and 2000-2019 for supply drive a supply model with medical-school graduates per 100,000 people, emigrating physicians and foreign physicians as regressors, and a demand model with GDP per capita, the out-of-pocket share of health expenditure and the over-65 population share, fitted with XGBoost, random forest, LSTM and Facebook Prophet under walk-forward validation and scored by RMSE. Because annual data leaves too few points for machine learning, the authors generate synthetic replicas with the Synthetic Data Vault and repeat the entire exercise on them, producing 100,000 observations for each of the supply and demand sets and trying 2,000- and 10,000-observation variants to check whether size changes the similarity scores. On real data XGBoost has the lowest error and puts 2030 supply at 3.04 and demand at 3.12 physicians per 1,000 people; on synthetic data LightGBM and gradient boosting give 2.03 and 2.86, agreeing with the real-data result on the direction of the gap, which is the paper's headline finding. The entry records SDV as the source of that synthetic half of the study: the sdv.tabular.GaussianCopula model is named as the generator, the enter-data-and-schemas then fit then sample workflow is described from SDV's own documentation, the PAR model is noted for the time-series case, and SDV's evaluate function supplies both the similarity scores and the metric table in the appendix.
evidence: the introduction states that it was foreseen that the number of available data points was slightly low for ML approaches, hence synthetic data was produced by using the synthetic data vault (SDV), and that using data similarity tests it was confirmed that synthetic data and real data were statistically similar; the synthetic data section states that one of these methods is the SDV, that the sdv.tabular.GaussianCopula model is based on the copula function, that a copula is a uniform distribution on the unit interval to the power d from which the multivariate normal distribution is built by the probability integral transform, and that the GaussianCopula model learns the data set and produces synthetic data in the same format and with the same statistical properties, cited to MIT Data to AI Lab 2018; the same section states that after the user enters the data and schemas into the SDV library the model is fitted to the data, synthetic data is generated from the fitted model, and it can be saved as a Python file with the .pkl extension, with figure 4 (Organize / Specify Structure / Learn Model / Synthesize Data) credited to Patki, Wedge and Veeramachaneni 2016; the following subsection states that in the SDV library there is a specially developed PAR model for time series data and that the PAR (Probabilistic AutoRegressive) model is used for multivariate time series; the results state that the SDV library was used for synthetic data generation alongside scikit-learn, TensorFlow, Keras, Prophet and PyCaret, that due to the paucity of the original data synthetic data with 100,000 observations was produced for both the supply and demand data sets, and that the evaluate function has been developed in the SDV library to evaluate the similarities between synthetic and original data, performing tests such as the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and averaging them, scoring 0.5554 for physician supply and 0.4779 for physician demand where 0 is worst and 1 best; appendix A tables A1 and A2 list the SDV comparison metrics used (logistic detection, SVC detection, Gaussian mixture log likelihood, KS test, KS test extended, continuous Kullback-Leibler divergence)

title: Artificial Intelligence Generated Synthetic Datasets as the Remedy for Data Scarcity in Water Quality Index Estimation
summary: Addresses data scarcity in water-quality-index estimation for two rivers in Peninsular Malaysia, the Selangor and the Skudai, where the Department of Environment's monthly sampling leaves only 240 points per river over 2005-2014, a shortage the authors argue is structural in developing regions and unresolved by bootstrap aggregation or adaptive synthetic sampling. Four generative methods, CTGAN, TVAE, the Gaussian copula and CopulaGAN, each produce a small synthetic set equal in size to the real data and a large one three times its size, shuffled with the real data; pairwise correlation difference, Kullback-Leibler divergence and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic select CopulaGAN at the Selangor River and TVAE at the Skudai River, with CTGAN and the plain Gaussian copula the weakest of the four, which the authors attribute to CTGAN suiting categorical data better than continuous water-quality variables. Back-propagation neural networks trained on the winning synthetic sets outperform those trained on real data across six input combinations ordered by SHAP importance, most sharply at the Selangor River, where mean absolute percentage error on the dissolved-oxygen-only input falls from 7.4 to 3.0 percent; dissolved oxygen is the most important variable at both rivers and at least two variables are needed at the Skudai. The entry records those four generators as the source of every synthetic row in the study: they are exactly the SDV tabular synthesizer set, with CTGAN and TVAE cited to Xu et al. and CopulaGAN described as a CTGAN variant carrying the copula CDF mechanism, and the whole contribution rests on training and sampling them.
evidence: the abstract states that four synthetic data generation methods, namely the conditional tabular generative adversarial network (CTGAN), the tabular variational autoencoder (TVAE), the Gaussian copula (GC) and the copula generative adversarial network (CopulaGAN), were used to synthesise datasets based on the real dataset; section 2.3.1 states that CTGAN was invented by Xu et al. (2019) to overcome the disadvantages of the GAN, that mode-specific normalisation using a variational Gaussian mixture model is integrated into the network and suits datasets with complicated distributions, and that a training-by-sampling approach avoids misrepresentation of the data, with the generated sets labelled CTGAN1 (real data shuffled with a synthetic set of the same size) and CTGAN2 (three times the size); section 2.3.2 states that the TVAE was also introduced by Xu et al. (2019) together with the CTGAN, with an encoder and decoder trained on the evidence lower-bound loss, and that the authors use the network structure proposed there; section 2.3.3 describes the Gaussian copula transforming each marginal into a normal distribution; section 2.3.4 states that CopulaGAN is a variant of the CTGAN in which the CDF mechanism is integrated and can be viewed as a combination of GC and CTGAN, retaining column correlation as much as possible; table 1 reports PCD, KLD and KS for all eight synthetic sets, CTGAN1 being the worst at the Selangor River (0.9969 / 1.9899 / 0.2322) against CopulaGAN1 at 0.3929 / 0.7695 / 0.1225; section 3.1 states that the CTGAN and GC appeared to have poorer performance than the TVAE and CopulaGAN, citing Inan et al. (2022) that CTGAN's nature is more suitable for categorical data; table 3 reports BPNN performance trained on real versus synthetic data at both rivers. NOTE: neither SDV nor sdv-dev is named anywhere in the paper, and the CopulaGAN description is cited to Bourou et al. 2021 rather than to any library; the four-method set is nonetheless the SDV tabular synthesizer API, and CopulaGAN is distributed only there, which is what keys this entry to the library as well as to CTGAN

title: Enhancing network intrusion detection: a dual-ensemble approach with CTGAN-balanced data and weak classifiers
summary: Attacks the class imbalance in UNSW-NB15, where intrusion records are far fewer than normal traffic and models trained on the raw set skew toward the majority class, with a two-stage label-wise stacking ensemble. Three deliberately weak binary classifiers, a decision tree, logistic regression and Gaussian naive Bayes, are trained per attack label on both the original and a balanced copy of the data; the best model per label feeds nine per-label XGBoost models, and a final XGBoost meta-classifier sits on top, reaching 98 percent accuracy on binary and 95 percent on multi-class classification, against the 93.88 percent binary and 80.96 percent multi-class figures of the ensemble study whose Chi-square feature selection the authors reuse for comparability. The balancing step generates CTGAN samples for every attack category up to 93,000 rows, matching the count of normal traffic, and the paper gives CTGAN its own methods section covering mode-specific normalisation via the variational Gaussian mixture model, the conditional vector and training-by-sampling, and the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty objective. Decision-tree and naive-Bayes base classifiers improve on nearly every attack label once the data is balanced while logistic regression proves largely insensitive to imbalance, and the authors read the reduced false-positive count as the practically important gain for an intrusion detection system. The entry records CTGAN as the generator of every synthetic row in the study, named in the paper's title and presented as its main contribution to the literature.
evidence: the abstract states that the main contribution to the existing literature is the introduction of a conditional tabular generative adversarial network (CTGAN) aimed at addressing the existing issue of data imbalance in the dataset, and that three shallow binary classification algorithms are trained on both the CTGAN-balanced data and the original imbalanced dataset; the introduction states that the authors introduced the CTGAN model as a novel solution to the pervasive issue of data imbalance present in UNSW-NB15 and that by utilizing CTGAN they effectively generated synthetic data, thereby balancing the dataset; section 3.3 states that in 2018 Xu and Veeramachaneni presented TGAN for producing artificial tabular data and that later, building on this, Xu et al. introduced CTGAN as an enhancement to TGAN, that CTGAN comprises a generator and discriminator trained in a zero-sum manner with extra details fed to both to condition generation on particular response variables, that the algorithm uses the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty as its loss, that the central element is re-sampling rows so all categories are equally distributed with the synthetic sample paired to the real value by the conditional distribution Pg(row given Ci = k), and that mode-specific normalisation distinguishes CTGAN from similar algorithms by handling non-Gaussian and multimodal distributions, implemented as identify continuous columns with the variational Gaussian mixture model, compute probability density, then sample a mode and normalise; section 4.1 states that the approach to balancing each attack label was to add synthetic data generated using CTGAN until the number of samples reached 93,000, equal to the number of normal samples, and that the CTGAN approach to balance the data was successful in all of the decision tree models; figures 3 and 4 contrast the raw label counts (Worms 174, Backdoor 2329, Normal 93,000) with 93,000 for every label after balancing; section 5.1 states that leveraging CTGAN-generated data lets the IDS learn from a diverse and realistic dataset. NOTE: no library or package is named for CTGAN anywhere in the paper, and the inline citation for CTGAN as an oversampling technique points to reference 14, the Bourou et al. GAN review, rather than to Xu et al., which is reference 29 and is cited correctly elsewhere
